Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 104, verse 1:

(p-198) Surat al-Humazah (سُورَةُ الهُمَزَةِ)

Makki, and its verses number nine.

﴿Woe﴾ (وَيْلٌ) is a mubtada' (subject), and its khabar (predicate) is ﴿to every backbiter, slanderer﴾ (لِكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُمَزَةٍ). The beginning with it is permissible even though it is nakira (indefinite), because it is a supplication against them for ruin or for severe evil. Al-hamz (الهَمْزُ) is breaking, like al-hazm (الهَزْمُ), and al-lamz (اللَّمْزُ) is faultfinding, like al-lahz (اللَّهْزُ). Both have come to be used for breaking people's honor and for defaming them. The pattern fu'alah (فُعَلَةٌ) indicates that this is a continuous habit to which the person has become accustomed, as also with al-lu'anah (اللُّعَنَةُ) and al-duhakah (الضُّحَكَةُ). It has been read as "لِكُلِّ هُمْزَةٍ لُمْزَةٍ" with the mim sukun (لُمْزَةٍ with sukun on the mim), and this is al-maskharah (المَسْخَرَةُ), the one who brings out jokes so that people laugh at him and mock him. It was said that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shurayq, for he was addicted to backbiting and disparagement. It was also said that it was about Ummayah ibn Khalaf, and it was said about al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and his slandering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his belittling of his exalted station. The specificity of the cause does not require that the threat be limited to them; rather, everyone who is characterized by their ugly attribute has sins of the same kind as theirs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 104, verse 2:

﴿The one who gathered wealth﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "kull" (every), or in the accusative, or in the nominative by way of censure (dhamm). It is also read "jamma'a" with the intensive doubling (tashdid), for abundance. The indefinite "mālan" (wealth) is for magnification and abundance, in agreement with His words, exalted is He: ﴿and counted it﴾. It has been said: the meaning of "addadahu" (counted it) is: he made it a store (iddah) against the calamities of time. It is also read "wa-'adadahu," meaning: he gathered the wealth and kept its count; or, he gathered his wealth and counted his supporters, from your saying: "Fulān dhū 'uddatin wa-'adadin" (so-and-so has a store and a number), when he has a large number of helpers and aides. It has also been said that it is a past-tense verb with the doubling unfolded (fakk al-idghām).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 104, verse 3:

﴿He thinks that his wealth will make him immortal.﴾ That is, he acts as one who supposes that his wealth will keep him alive. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun (al-iẓhar fi mawqi' al-iḍmar) is for the sake of emphasis (li-ziyadat al-taqrir). It has also been said: his wealth lengthened his hope and filled him with distant wishes, so that, from the extremity of his heedlessness and the length of his hope, he comes to think that wealth has left him to live forever in this world, never dying. It has also been said: this is an allusion to righteous action and renunciation of the world, and that it is righteous action that makes its doer immortal in the everlasting life and enduring bliss, whereas wealth is neither immortal nor makes anyone immortal. It is related that al-Akhnas had four thousand dinars, and it is said ten thousand. The sentence is either a new (resumptive) clause (mustaʼnifah) or a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the subject of "jama'a" (he gathered).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 104, verse 4:

﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke to him for (p-199)

that vain reckoning. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿he will surely be thrown﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, and the clause is a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining the cause of the rebuke, i.e.: By God, he will surely be cast off because of his engagement in the deeds mentioned.

﴿into the Crushing (al-Hutamah)﴾, i.e., into the Fire, whose nature is to crush and break everything thrown into it, just as his own nature is to tear down people's honor and amass wealth.
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what al-Hutamah is?﴾ is to magnify its matter by making clear that it is not among the things that the minds of creation can grasp.

Allah's "And His saying: ﴿It is the Fire of Allah﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is an explanation (bayan) of the matter of that about which one is asked, i.e., it is: the fire of Allah, kindled by the command of Allah, the Mighty in authority. In its attribution to Him, glorified is He, and in describing it as kindled (al-iqad), there is a magnification of its matter beyond which there is no further increase."

Note: the translation above has a flaw in its opening clause, which I should correct: the Arabic opens with "وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى" ("And His, exalted is He, saying"), so the accurate rendering is:

"And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is the Fire of Allah﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is an explanation (bayan) of the matter of that about which one is asked, i.e., it is: the fire of Allah, kindled by the command of Allah, the Mighty in authority. In its attribution to Him, glorified is He, and in describing it as kindled (al-iqad), there is a magnification of its matter beyond which there is no further increase."

﴿Which mounts over the hearts﴾. That is: it rises up to the middle of the hearts and envelops them. Its being singled out for mention is because the fu'ad (heart/inner core) is the most delicate part of the body and the most sensitive to pain from the slightest harm that touches it. Or it is because it is the locus of deviant beliefs, of wicked intentions, and the source of evil deeds.
Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾. That is: sealed shut, from awṣadtu al-bāb and aṣadtuhu, meaning I closed the door.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 104, verse 9:

﴿In extended pillars﴾. It may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronominal suffix in "عَلَيْهِمْ" ('alayhim, "upon them"), meaning: they are situated in extended pillars, that is, bound therein like the stocks (maqāṭir) in which thieves are put in fetters. Or it may be the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: they are in pillars. Or it may be an attribute of "مُؤْصَدَةٌ" (mu'ṣada, "closed"), as Abu al-Baqa' said, meaning: it is closed, with its doors shut upon them and the pillars extended across the doors, for added security upon security. O Allah, protect us from it, O best of those sought for protection. It is also read "عُمُدٍ" ('umud) with two dammas.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Humaza, Allah the Exalted will grant him ten good deeds for every person who mocked Muhammad and his Companions."
